title: Quantum computers
reading: In 1982 Richard Feynman observes that simulating quantum systems on ordinary calculating machines requires resources growing exponentially with the number of particles, and proposes machines built from quantum-mechanical elements. In 1985 David Deutsch describes a universal quantum computer. In 1994 Peter Shor shows that such a machine could factor large numbers efficiently — which would break the codes that protect most electronic communication. Building one is extraordinarily hard, because the superpositions must be protected from their surroundings. In 2019 a group at Google reports a 53-element processor completing a specialised sampling task they estimate would take a classical supercomputer thousands of years; improved classical methods later narrow the gap.
detail: The resource is the exponentially large space of joint states of many two-state systems, together with interference. Error correction (from 1995) makes large machines possible in principle; demonstrations of error-corrected logical elements below threshold appeared from 2023.

claim.label: The formalism does the work
claim.summary: Speculative. No evidence of Dirac's views on computation; the voice extrapolates from transformation theory.
voice: Then the space of states is doing the calculation. That is not surprising if one takes the formalism seriously. It would be surprising only to someone who thought the formalism was a description of something simpler.

claim.label: Where does the calculation happen?
voice: If the machine truly explores more possibilities than there are particles in it, I should like to know where that exploration takes place. That is the same question I have been asking all week in another form.
claim.reasoning: Demands a realistic account of the resource.

claim.label: The waves are real enough
voice: A machine that computes with interference of waves in configuration space. I was told the wave was only a bookkeeping device. It appears the bookkeeping can be put to work.

claim.label: Probabilities at the end
voice: I note the machine's answer is still read out with probabilities. The art must be to arrange the amplitudes so the right answer is the likely one.
